lines.caption: This is a tour of pull request 8, which builds Thunar's .debs in CI on every PR and publishes a release on every merge.
It has three parts: what this PR adds, how it was built and verified, and what comes later.
Part 1. What this PR adds.
It starts when a PR into main is opened or updated. A new push cancels the older run.
The build job compiles Thunar on Ubuntu with Zorin's PPA, and dry-runs the release scripts.
The five .debs are kept for 14 days as an artifact, and the PR gets a green check.
lines.say: The five debs are kept for fourteen days as an artifact, and the PR gets a green check.

lines.caption: You review and merge. That is the only gate before a release exists.
The merge is a push to main, which runs the workflow again, one run at a time.
A script stamps the version: the highest local number so far, plus one.
The build job runs again, now with the real version in the changelog.
The release job publishes the release with three of the five .debs, and keeps the newest ten.
lines.say: The release job publishes the release with three of the five debs, and keeps the newest ten.

lines.caption: Your machines run installed packages, not source code. This PR has GitHub build those packages for you.
One workflow file drives it all. It runs on two events: a pull request, and a push to main.
Steps one and two: GitHub lends a fresh Ubuntu machine, adds Zorin's libraries, and compiles the PR.
Step three keeps the .debs at the placeholder version +local0, so apt would never install them by accident.
lines.say: Step three keeps the debs at a placeholder version, local zero, so apt would never install them by accident.

lines.caption: Step four is you: read the changes, check that the build is green, and merge.
Steps five and six: the merge starts the workflow again, and the next version is written only on the build machine.
Steps seven and eight: the same build, then a separate job, the only one allowed to write, publishes the release.
To roll back, delete the bad release. The updater will then install the previous one.
The packaging is Zorin's, with four edits. It bootstraps from git, and sets the plugin path without a patch.
The changelog starts at +local0, and Thunar's own test passes again.
lines.say: The changelog starts at local zero, and Thunar's own test passes again.

lines.caption: This is the edit to the package's build rules: bootstrap with autogen, and two configure options.
The PR adds the packaging, one workflow, and three release scripts.
The first release is +local2, each one after adds one, and the count goes on when upstream moves.
lines.say: The first release is local two, each one after adds one, and the count goes on when upstream moves.

lines.caption: Part 2. How it was built and verified.
It was built from Zorin's packaging, compared with your hand build, and built from git, not the tarball.
A local build matched your hand build: same files, same dependencies, same plugin path, and the test passed.
CI built it too, before the review fixes, and its packages matched as well.
The version, pruning and publishing scripts were run against mocked releases and a fake GitHub client.
Nothing was installed on the desktop during any of this.
A code review of the whole diff at extra high found eleven issues, and all of them are fixed.
The main ones: releases could reuse or go back to an old version, and every PR could see the GitHub token.
The release job itself only runs after the first merge, and the version check after the second.
Part 3. What comes later: issue 7, then issue 2.
In issue 7, a cloud agent opens the PR, CI builds and verifies it, and you merge.
In issue 2, each machine checks for a new release every hour, installs it, and asks you to restart Thunar.
Issue 7 adds the repo's instructions, the screenshot skills, a verify job, and a sandbox check.
Issue 2 adds an updater on a timer, which installs the new packages and never restarts Thunar for you.
That's the tour: every PR now builds Thunar's packages, and every merge publishes them as a release.
